explanation: All of China keeps Beijing time, although the country is wide enough to span five time zones. In the far west, winter sunrises come very late in the morning.

claims.text: China officially uses a single time zone, Beijing time.
China does not officially use two, four or five time zones.
China's land stretches across five nominal one-hour time zones.
In far western China, winter sunrise comes very late in the morning by Beijing time.

writerNotes: Self-check (§9.3). Lint: content:check run for the batch and writer; no errors or warnings on this item. Claims: every checkable statement is listed, distractors included; c1 (number), c2 (number) and c3 (number) are high under the C26 floor, and c4 is standard. Datasets: natural-earth ne_110m_admin_0_countries ADM0_A3=CHN: the polygon runs from about 73.7 E to 135.0 E, which touches the five 15-degree zones centred on 75, 90, 105, 120 and 135 E (c3). No dataset states the official time zone. Rival test: Five is the planted trap, the number China's width suggests; two and four are plausible middle answers. Against the key: some people in the far west keep an unofficial local time two hours behind Beijing, which is why the stem says 'officially'. Volatility: slow, because a time-zone rule is government policy that could change, although China's single zone dates from 1949. The schema requires a reviewBy date for slow items, so I entered 1 October 2028 as a suggestion; the editor sets the final date at acceptance. Regional: Nobody's local knowledge outside China; the surprise works everywhere. Style: Oxford spelling, plain hyphens only, straight apostrophes, explanation of 29 words. External evidence: c1 and c2 need a Tier A or B web result (one search covers both). Seed: 5 (hard): most players guess several zones; the counterintuitive truth is a single one. Counterintuitive: true; the obvious answer is wrong, as the rival test explains, and the explanation defuses it. Doubts: none.

Nominal zones are 15° wide, centred on multiples of 15°: 73.7° E falls in UTC+5 (67.5 to 82.5° E) and 135.0° E in UTC+9 (127.5 to 142.5° E), so China spans five (UTC+5 to UTC+9). The 1:110m outline is generalized, but both ends sit far inside their zones.

evidence.restatement: Kashgar, near 76° E, is about three hours of solar time behind Beijing's meridian, so its midwinter sunrise comes around 10 am Beijing time.
China officially uses one standard time, UTC+8 (Beijing Time), nationwide.

claimResults.note: High-risk number. Knowledge only (no web search was available to me); counts only with external evidence from pass A (guide 9.5.3). The word 'officially' in the stem covers Xinjiang's unofficial local time.

issues.note: The explanation says 'All of China keeps Beijing time', but in Xinjiang many residents also use an unofficial local time two hours behind. The stem is safe because it says 'officially'; the explanation would be safer as 'Officially, all of China keeps Beijing time'.
